catalog_citation: Svantesson, Jan-Olof. 1991. Hu - a language with unorthodox tonogenesis. In J.H.C.S. Davidson (ed.), Austroasiatic Languages: Essays in honour of H. L. Shorto, 67-79. London: SOAS. (SEAlang SALA archive PDF)
catalog_locator: p.67 (introduction), p.69 (Minor syllables), p.71 (Tones and vowels)
catalog_quote: p.67: From a general phonological point of view, the most interesting phenomenon is the development of a two-tone system where the tones are not the reflexes of voiced/voiceless proto-initials, as is most often the case in Mon-Khmer two-tone (or two-register) languages. Instead, the tones are the reflexes of the long/short vowel opposition which existed in Proto-Palaungic (inherited from Proto-Mon-Khmer). ... p.69: Minor syllables. As in other Northern Mon-Khmer languages, most non-compound words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, i.e. consisting of a major syllable preceded by an unstressed minor syllable (cf. Shorto 1960). Minor syllables have a syllabic sonorant (such as m in θmphúp 'lung') or a (probably) non-contrasting vowel which I have written as a (kaʔà 'two'). ... p.71: Tones and vowels. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three deciding passages (pp.67, 69, 71) are verbatim at the stated pages in the SEAlang scan we hold of Svantesson 1991 (read as page scan; no text). (2) Deciding source: a 1991 phonology article by Svantesson from a small one-speaker vocabulary; primary and competent, but not the fullest description - Glottolog lists a 226-pp 2016 reference grammar in Mandarin (Jiang & Shi, Kunge = Hu) and a 2004 Minzu Yuwen sketch (Li Jinfang), and Wikipedia cites Sidwell 2015 pp.49-50 for a syllable template with stress on the major syllable and presyllables 'always unstressed', which agrees with our classification. (3) No open copy of any of these could be downloaded: for the session was exhausted, DuckDuckGo/Semantic Scholar/WorldCat downloads were refused (connection refused / 429), Bing returned irrelevant results; the three works still to obtain are print-only or CNKI. sources.citation: Hsiu, Andrew. 2015. The Angkuic languages: a preliminary survey. Handout prepared for ICAAL 6 (6th International Conference on Austroasiatic Linguistics), Siem Reap, Cambodia, July 29-31, 2015. 12 pp. Zenodo (deposited 2017-12-23, with comparative wordlist spreadsheets). doi:10.5281/zenodo.1127808
sources.note: Secondhand, one line: p.1 'Background: All Angkuic languages are tonal (cf. Svantesson 1988, 1991).' Hu is classed as Southern Angkuic; Hu forms in the comparative tables carry Chao tone numbers taken from Li 2006 and Svantesson 1991 (listed as the Hu sources, p.9); no tone inventory or analysis for Hu. Also notes Hu (Li 2006) is one of three Angkuic languages with >1,000 lexical items documented.

sources.note: First-hand comparative tonogenesis study: Hu has developed a tone system independently of its relatives; in Hu tone development is connected with the merger of long and short vowels (vs. voiced/voiceless initial merger in Kammu, Blang, Lamet and vowel-length/other mergers in U), explained through universal microprosodic properties of segments. Expected to give the Hu two-tone (high/low) inventory with phonetic data; multi-language article, Hu is one of four case studies.
